To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
there is a cancer value of a statistical risk that is greater than that for acute fatalities.
the value of a life with cancer is $10.8m and is 21% larger than the value of a statistically equivalent life without cancer.
the value of a life saved from cancer is $11.1 million and is 21% higher than the value of a statistically average life.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the valuation of a statistical life in the context of a cancer premium.
the valuation of cancer risks, which are often considered to be the most feared of all risks.
the question: how much is a cancer case worth?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a cancer value of a statistical risk that is significantly different to the value of a non-cancer risk.
the cancer premium is greater than the median VSL but less than the cancer VSL proposed for policy analyses.
there is evidence for a cancer premium, but that it is not as large as the cancer premium proposed for policy analysis in the USA and UK.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is a cancer value premium that is smaller than the value premium proposed for policy analysis in other countries.
the value of a life with a 50% probability of developing cancer is 21% higher than the value of a statistically average life.
cancer risk premiums are not large enough to warrant a separate valuation of cancer risk in cost–benefit analyses.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the value of reducing cancer risks to zero is greater than the value of reducing risks of death to zero, which suggests that cancer risk reductions may have a greater value than risk reductions for acute fatalities.
the value of a life lost to cancer is greater than that of an acute death, although it is not as large as some policy analysts have suggested.
there are substantial premiums for cancer risks in stated preferences.
